item.title: Extension complexity is not additive under Cartesian products
item.description: arXiv:2611.33631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the linear extension complexity of a Cartesian product of polytopes can be strictly smaller than the sum of the extension complexities of its factors. This disproves Conjecture 1.2 of Grande, Padrol and Sanyal. We construct a rational 24-dimensional polytope $P$ with 50 facets and 150 vertices such that $P$ has extension complexity 40 and $P \times P$ has extension complexity exactly 79. We also prove that the saving can be arbitrarily large, even in a Cartesian square: for every $t$ there is a rational polytope $R_t$ whose square needs at least $t$ fewer inequalities than two separate copies of $R_t$. For two different factors, we construct a family whose product saves at least $\lceil 5n/27 \rceil$ inequalities while the two separate complexities sum to $O(n)$, so that the saving is a constant fraction of the total. The proofs rest on a transfer theorem: wedging over the omitted facets of a polytope turns a gap between the nonnegative ranks of partial slack matrices into a gap between extension complexities. The unbounded squares come from intersecting families of sets on successively larger alphabets. In the square the two copies of each coordinate share generators, while a counting lemma determines the exact cost of a single factor.
item.dc:creator: Minhao Liu

item.title: Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: Constructions and Upper Bounds for Trifferent Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.33212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A ternary code of blocklength $n$ is trifferent if every three distinct codewords have a coordinate at which they take all three values. Let $T(n)$ be the largest size of such a code. We prove that $T(n)=\Omega(1.162579^n)$ and $T(n)=O(n^{-1/2}(3/2)^n)$. The lower bound improves the exponential base $(9/5)^{1/4}=1.15829\ldots$ of K\"orner and Marton. It comes from a random system of overlapping local constraints, in which every position is read two or three times, followed by thinning and the deletion of nearby pairs and of the remaining triples that violate trifference. The required estimates reduce to finitely many inequalities, which we verify rigorously by computer. The upper bound improves our earlier bound $O(n^{-2/5}(3/2)^n)$.
item.dc:creator: Siddharth Bhandari, Abhishek Khetan

item.title: Fast Algorithms for Permanents of Permutationally-Dominant Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.33485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a fast algorithm for approximating the permanent of permutationally-dominant matrices. In particular, we obtain a fully polynomial randomised approximation scheme whose runtime is quadratic in both the dimension of the matrix and the inverse of the approximation error. Our approach is based on a polymer model representation of the permanent and importance sampling of the logarithm of its partition function via the theory of heaps of pieces of Viennot.
item.dc:creator: Ryan L. Mann

item.title: Tighter Upper Bounds on Distinct $k$-Powers via Left Lyndon Trees
item.description: arXiv:2602.12711v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A $k$-power is a word of the form $x^{k}$ for a non-empty word $x$; a $2$-power is called a square. Li, Pachocki and Radoszewski [Electron. J. Comb., 2024] proved that the number of distinct $k$-powers in a word $w$ of length $n$ with $\sigma$ distinct letters is at most $\frac{n - \sigma}{k-1}$. In this paper, we lower the bound to $\frac{1}{k-1}\left( n - \sigma - \log_{2} n + O(\log (k (\sigma + \log n))) \right)$. For $k = 2$ this improves the bound $n - \Theta(\log n)$ of Brlek and Li [WORDS, 2023] by an additive $\sigma$ and makes the constant hidden in $\Theta(\log n)$ explicit. Unlike previous work, which compares cycle lengths with the order of the Rauzy graph, our proof classifies cycles by Lyndon words. Given a long Lyndon word $z$ all of whose conjugates occur in $w$, it extracts $\log_{2}|z|$ extra cycles that carry no $k$-power, one for each node of the left Lyndon tree of $z$.
item.dc:creator: Eitatsu Tomita, Peaker Guo, Tomohiro I

item.title: Infinite families of planar graphs of a given injective chromatic number
item.description: arXiv:2412.09969v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An injective colouring of a graph is a colouring in which every two vertices sharing a common neighbour receive a different colour. Chen, Hahn, Raspaud and Wang conjectured that every planar graph of maximum degree $\Delta \ge 3$ admits an injective colouring with at most $\lceil 3\Delta/2\rceil$ colours. This was later disproved by Lu\v{z}ar and \v{S}krekovski for certain small and even values of $\Delta$ and they proposed a new refined conjecture. Using an algorithm for determining the injective chromatic number of a graph, i.e. the smallest number of colours for which the graph admits an injective colouring, we give computational evidence for Lu\v{z}ar and \v{S}krekovski's conjecture and extend their results by presenting an infinite family of $3$-connected planar graphs for each $\Delta$ (except for $4$) attaining their bound, whereas they only gave a finite amount of examples for each $\Delta$. Hence, together with another infinite family of maximum degree $4$, we provide infinitely many counterexamples to the conjecture by Chen et al. for each $\Delta$ if $4\le \Delta \le 7$ and every even $\Delta \ge 8$. We provide similar evidence for analogous conjectures by La and \v{S}torgel and Lu\v{z}ar, \v{S}krekovski and Tancer when the girth is restricted as well. Also in these cases we provide infinite families of $3$-connected planar graphs attaining the bounds of these conjectures for certain maximum degrees $\Delta\geq 3$.
item.dc:creator: Matias Daneels, Jan Goedgebeur, Jarne Renders

item.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Coloring Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.09837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coloring Discovery asks whether a possibly improper initial coloring can be made proper within a prescribed number of allowed changes. We study the parameterized complexity of three modification step models that were studied previously in the literature: recoloring one vertex (color flipping), swapping the colors of arbitrary vertices (color swapping), and swapping colors only across an edge (color sliding). For color flipping, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for the parameters vertex cover and distance to complete. For color swapping, we obtain fixed-parameter tractability for the parameter vertex cover plus the number of colors. Our lower bounds show W[1]-hardness for treedepth plus feedback vertex set in the color flipping model and for the number of colors plus bandwidth or distance to disjoint paths in the swapping and sliding models. All three variants remain NP-complete with four colors on graphs of diameter two.
item.dc:creator: Eric Decker, Sebastian Siebertz

item.title: List packing for graphs with small arboricity
item.description: arXiv:2611.24832v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that every graph $G$ whose edge set is the union of $r$ forests has list packing number at most $2^r$. This means that for all $k\ge 2^r$ and every list-assignment $L$ with lists of size $k$, the graph $G$ admits $k$ disjoint proper $L$-colourings. While for large $r$ this bound is far from optimal, for $r\in\{1,2\}$ it is sharp. As a direct corollary of the case $r=2$, we obtain that every triangle-free planar graph has list packing number at most $4$, thus improving upon a result of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Masa\v{r}\'ik, Mus\'ilek and Pangr\'ac and providing the optimal answer to a question of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Postle and Norin on (weighted) $\epsilon$-flexibility of such graphs. As a corollary of the case $r=3$, we obtain a short alternative proof that every $K_5$-minor-free (and hence every planar) graph has list-packing number at most $8$, matching the state of the art. All results above also hold for the stronger notion of correspondence packing.
item.dc:creator: Stijn Cambie, Wouter Cames van Batenburg, Xuding Zhu
